A sequin is a tiny, flat, round, shiny disc used as decoration on clothing and accessories. Think of it as a miniature, glittering coin — but made for fashion, not for spending.

A sequin is very small, usually about the size of a fingernail or smaller. It is flat and circular, like a tiny disc or coin. It has a small hole — typically in the center or near one edge — through which a thread can pass. This hole is what allows it to be stitched onto a surface.

The key quality of a sequin is that it is highly reflective. Its surface is shiny and smooth, almost like a mirror, so when light hits it, it catches and bounces the light back in a glittery, sparkling way.

Modern sequins are most commonly made of plastic, though they can also be made of metal, metallic foil, or other reflective materials. They come in virtually every color — gold and silver are the most classic, but you will find them in red, blue, green, black, holographic rainbow, and so on.

Sequins are used purely for decoration. They are sewn onto fabric — one by one, or in large clusters — to make an item of clothing or an accessory look glamorous, festive, and eye-catching. When hundreds or thousands of sequins are stitched onto a garment, the entire surface shimmers and glitters as the person moves, because each tiny disc catches light from a slightly different angle.

You will most commonly see sequins on:

  • Clothing: Party dresses, evening gowns, tops, skirts, and jackets. A heavily sequined dress is often described as a "sequin dress" or "sequined dress." Performers on stage or in films often wear such outfits because sequins catch stage lighting dramatically.
  • Costumes: Dancers, especially in styles like ballroom dancing, Latin dance, or showgirl performances, frequently wear costumes covered in sequins.
  • Accessories: Handbags, shoes, belts, headbands, and even phone cases can be decorated with sequins.
  • Festive items: During celebrations, holidays, or carnivals, sequined decorations on clothing and party items are very common.

The defining visual effect of sequins is sparkle. Because each sequin is a reflective disc, and because they are typically used in groups, the collective result is a surface that seems to twinkle and shimmer constantly — especially under bright or moving light. This is why sequined garments feel energetic and celebratory. Even the slightest movement of the wearer causes dozens of these tiny discs to shift angles simultaneously, creating an almost living, dancing quality to the light.

One piece is called a sequin. When referring to many of them (as is almost always the case in real life), you say sequins. The adjective form is sequined (also spelled sequinned), meaning "decorated with sequins" — as in, a sequined jacket or sequined shoes.

In a nutshell: A sequin is a small, flat, shiny decorative disc with a hole in it, sewn onto fabric to make it sparkle and shimmer. It is a building block of glamour in fashion and performance.
